summary: Defines the basic principle of establishing a mesh in which interoperating directory services exchange index objects, using the Common Indexing Protocol. It reports results from the TISDAG project.

plainLanguage.summary: Directory gateways can be linked to each other so that a search at one of them reaches data held by providers registered with another. They do this by exchanging index objects, which summarise what each provider can answer. This memo describes that exchange, the three ways two services can be joined, and the questions that were still open when it was written.

questions: how do directory gateways form a mesh
subtitle: How directory gateways can be linked to each other, so a search at one of them reaches data held behind another.

tldr.problem: TISDAG built a single directory access gateway serving one region or country. Serving several gateways needs a way for them to exchange index information, so that a search started at one of them can reach data held anywhere in the group.
tldr.mechanism: Each DAG server aggregates the index objects of the providers in front of it into one index object and exchanges that with the other servers. A query that matches another server's aggregate produces a referral to that server rather than to the individual providers behind it.
tldr.outcome: The memo works through three ways to join two services and lists the design questions that were still open, such as when a query should widen its scope. It is Informational, and reports experience from the TISDAG project.

facts.label: Mesh shapes described
facts.value: Hierarchical or graph-like, preferably without loops

today: RFC 2968 is an Informational memo reporting results from the TISDAG project, and the metadata does not list it as obsoleted or updated. The memo says experience with real server mesh topologies was still limited when it was written, and lists design questions that remained open. It is read alongside RFC 2967 and RFC 2969.

sections.title: From One Gateway to a Mesh
sections.content:
The Common Indexing Protocol, or CIP, was designed to create query referral indexes, and it can also create a mesh of loosely affiliated referral indexes. The purpose of such a mesh is to spread indexing and searching work across different servers. The TISDAG project had so far created a single referral index, and the memo treats the obvious next step: integrating that into a larger set of interoperating services.

Two extensions are possible. One is a mesh of DAG-based services, where DAG stands for Directory Access Gateway. The other is to use the mesh architecture to incorporate access to other types of service, such as the Norwegian Directory of Directories. Either way, the basic principle for establishing a mesh is that interoperating services should exchange index objects according to the shape of the mesh, which may be hierarchical or graph-like, preferably without loops.
sections.plainLanguage: One country had a directory gateway. The memo asks what happens when several countries each run one and want a search at any of them to reach every provider. The answer given is to exchange index objects between the gateways.

sections.title: How a Mesh Is Built
sections.content:
The memo proposes that the mesh be built from index objects aggregated over the servers of the participating services. Referrals are then generated to other recognised services, not to their individual providers. The important reason for not simply passing index objects forward unaggregated is that individual services may support different ranges of access protocols and may have particular security requirements, so a referral should be directed to a CAP, either the standard one used by the DAG system or a new one established to support the semantics of the remote system.

Within a given DAG system, a referral to a remote server looks just like any other referral, although a particular SAP may be established to provide query fulfillment. That SAP enables translations between variations of service, and allows secure access when the relationship between the services is restricted.

The key element for establishing a mesh of any sort is the exchange of the CIP index object, not the internal system architecture. The scenarios that follow assume the primary service is a DAG-based service, but in most cases they would apply just as well if the remote service were provided by some other kind of service architecture.
sections.plainLanguage: Each gateway summarises what its own providers can answer, and swaps that summary with the other gateways. A search that matches another gateway's summary produces a pointer to that gateway, not to the individual providers.

sections.title: Three Ways to Join Two Services
sections.content:
Assume that two countries tie their services together and a user makes a query in Country A. A certain number of hits are made against the index objects of A's providers, and there is also a hit in the aggregate index of Country B.

In Case 1 the two services are essentially the same in terms of protocols, queries and schema. One referral is generated per protocol supported by Country B's service. The referral can be passed back as far as the client if its protocol supports referrals, or the CAP can chain it through an appropriate SAP in the usual fashion. In other words, the CAPs of Country B's service act as providers to Country A's service.

In Case 2 the two services address the same service type, such as whitepages, but do not use an identical collection of protocols, allowed queries or schema. The index object that Country B sent to Country A's DAG service must then be constructed in terms of Country A's service, so that appropriate hits are generated against it. Resolving the referral then needs further protocol, schema and query mapping. That mapping can be done by a special SAP established inside Country A's service, or by a particular CAP that Country B establishes. The difference between the two approaches is who manages the relationship: Country A can handle it if it knows its own service as well as the published access to Country B, or Country B can be responsible for establishing a CAP for every country that wants to connect to it, which reduces the overhead on Country A's service.

Case 3 is a refinement of the first. If the two services are identical in every way except for the data they cover, it may make sense to copy Country B's index objects to Country A's server instead of aggregating them, and to give Country A's CAPs access to the SAPs of Country B so that chaining is carried out at the remote service. The memo says the answer does not come from technology: it depends entirely on the nature of the relationship that can be established between the two services.
sections.plainLanguage: There are three ways to connect two gateways. If they work the same way, a referral can pass straight through. If they differ, something has to translate between them. If they are identical apart from the data, one gateway can copy the other's index and query it directly.

sections.title: Widening the Scope of a Query
sections.content:
The scenario above assumes that Country A's server received index objects from Country B's server. That will be the case if Country A's server is higher in the levels of a hierarchy of services, or if the network is made up of servers that share their index objects with all others. In the latter case, searching at any one of the servers yields the full range of results, and referrals are made to any other server that might have data fulfilling the user's query. Sharing the index objects is a way to let each server manage local data while enabling distributed load-sharing on the basic query handling.

If a hierarchical, or at least not-completely-connected, model is used, a query carried out at a level other than the top of the hierarchy, or in one particular branch of it, will not be matched against all index objects. A user sending a query to Country B's service may be content to limit the scope to that country's information. The memo says this happens often enough in real life that the hierarchical relationship becomes an effective mechanism for scoping queries, instead of flooding the entire network with every single query or keeping full copies of all the data in every server.

The DAG/IP provides control constructs that let components act according to the topology of the mesh. A CAP might use the polled-by system command to establish which other servers in the mesh exist at higher levels, and would therefore be worth contacting if the scope of the search is to be increased. The memo lists the questions that needed more experience with real server mesh topologies: should the CAP always broaden the scope, or only if there are no local referrals, or only under user direction; should it use a local SAP to contact the remote service's CAP; and is it better to completely connect the mesh of servers or to produce some kind of hierarchy.
sections.plainLanguage: A query usually starts at one gateway. Whether it should then be sent further depends on the shape of the network and on what the user wants. The memo says the machinery for finding the higher levels exists, but that the rules for when to use it were not settled.

sections.title: Letting a Provider Decide
sections.content: Depending on the context in which a mesh is established, for example between national white pages services or between different units of a corporate organization, it may be useful to allow individual WDSPs to indicate whether they are willing to have their data included in a DAG system's aggregated index object. Including a provider's data is what allows the DAG system to receive referrals from other systems in the mesh, so a provider that does not want to take part in that wider federation can say so. The memo raises this as a consideration for whoever sets up a mesh, without specifying a mechanism.
sections.plainLanguage: A provider can be allowed to refuse to have its data summarised for the wider network. The memo mentions this as an option worth having, but does not say how it would work.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The memo says it describes different configurations for sharing information between information services, and that it introduces no security considerations beyond those attendant in, and addressed by, particular directory service access protocols. In other words, the security of the mesh depends on the access protocols the participating services already use, not on anything added by the mesh itself.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo adds no security of its own. Whatever protection the directory access protocols provide is what the mesh relies on.

viz.caption: THE QUERY, REFERRAL AND RESOLUTION SHOWN IN THE RFC

messages.label: QUERY
messages.note: The client asks Country A's DAG system for a match.

messages.label: REFERRAL
messages.note: Country A returns a referral based on the index object sent by Country B.

messages.label: RESOLUTION
messages.note: The client follows the referral straight to Country B's DAG system.

viz.caption: THE THREE CASES THE MEMO WORKS THROUGH

cells: Essentially the same protocols, queries and schema
One referral per protocol Country B supports, passed to the client or chained through a SAP
Same service type, different protocols, queries or schema
Mapping done by a special SAP in Country A, or by a CAP that Country B establishes
Identical except for the data covered
Index objects copied instead of aggregated, and Country A's CAPs use Country B's SAPs

viz.caption: THE DESIGN QUESTIONS THE MEMO LEAVES OPEN

items.title: When to widen the scope
items.text: Always, only when there are no local referrals, or only when the user asks.

items.title: Which path to use
items.text: A local SAP contacting the remote CAP, or a direct CAP to CAP connection.

items.title: What shape the mesh takes
items.text: Completely connected servers, or a hierarchy.

items.title: Which data is shared
items.text: A provider can refuse to have its data included in an aggregated index object.
